Book pages 596 to 601. Cisco's Unified Wireless Network (CUWN) was built to fix the problems of managing many APs one at a time: inconsistent security, interference, and channel planning. There are three models:
Each AP configured on its own
Small sites, branches without IT staff
APs work in this model. They run IOS with extra wireless features, and you configure each one separately.
A static site survey is a snapshot of the RF environment. RF changes constantly (a new neighbour, a new metal object), so the snapshot goes out of date.
Wireless Domain Services (WDS) and the older Wireless LAN Solution Engine (WLSE) added a little central control.
WDS and WLSE are legacy. The book mentions them in passing; you do not need them.
. The WLC pushes configuration to APs and tunes the radio environment in real time.
(Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points). Control uses
Client data in the tunnel carries RSSI and SNR information. Traffic goes to the WLC, so one central firewall can protect all wireless traffic.
AP and WLC exchange certificates and

The AP configuration lives only in
while connected, so removing the AP does not leak the configuration.
CUWN has five elements: client devices, APs, network unification, network management, mobility services.
Controller types named: WLC (AireOS), Mobility Express (runs on some APs or switches), and the
The book says CAPWAP carries control information "over an encrypted tunnel" and the summary says APs register through an "encrypted CAPWAP tunnel". Per Cisco documentation,
DTLS encrypts the control channel by default
data channel is not encrypted by default
. Data encryption (DTLS on UDP 5247) is optional and needs support on the AP and WLC. For the exam: control = UDP 5246 (encrypted), data = UDP 5247.

The book also lists the Wireless Control System (WCS) and the Wireless Location Appliance. These are older management products that were replaced by newer tools (Cisco Prime Infrastructure, then DNA Center). Treat them as history.
Cisco has been moving customers from AireOS controllers to the Catalyst 9800. The book's WLC commands are AireOS and look very different from IOS XE. I did not verify AireOS end-of-sale dates.
The lightweight model splits 802.11 MAC functions between the AP and the WLC. The AP does the
work; the WLC does the rest.
Handled by the lightweight AP (real time)
Handled by the WLC (not time sensitive)

Buffering and sending frames for power-save clients
Probe responses; relaying probe requests to the WLC
Termination of all 802.11 frames at the controller

RF channel monitoring: noise, interference, rogue APs
Layer 2 wireless encryption and decryption (except VPN and IPsec clients)
. Even though the WLC handles authentication, the WPA2 or EAP encryption keys remain in the AP and the client.
APs are managed entirely from the cloud. The AP only needs Internet reachability.
A control plane goes to the cloud for management and monitoring; the
, so user traffic is not affected by the cloud.
Downsides: no CLI on the APs, little local management, and if the Internet link is down you cannot change settings. Fewer features than controller-based Cisco gear.
Good fit for companies or branches with no skilled IT staff.
The sentence introducing Meraki in the book is garbled ("by using Cisco's APs - Donald. Meraki is entirely managed by the cloud"). It is a typo; Meraki is Cisco's cloud-managed product line.
